title: Courting by the Cornfield
pages:
Courting by the Cornfield
Hannah Stoltzfus had churned butter many times before.
But never like this.
Today… it felt different.
“Why does my heart beat so,” she whispered, gripping the churn handle with determination, “as though I have run all the way to the neighbor’s and back… twice?”
She knew the answer.
It was Eli Zook.
Eli, whose buggy wheels never squeaked.
Eli, whose suspenders were always perfectly… suspendin’.
Eli, who once fixed a crooked fence post with such precision 
that three grown men nodded in approval.
“Ach,” Hannah sighed. “He is… very capable.”
Meanwhile, down the lane, Eli Zook sat in his buggy, holding the reins with unusual intensity.
“Easy now, Buttercup,” he told his horse. “This is no ordinary visit.”
Buttercup neighed softly, as if understanding the gravity of the situation.
Eli nodded. “Ja. Today… I speak to Hannah.”
He adjusted his hat.
Then adjusted it again.
Then, for good measure… a third time.
“One must be presentable,” he muttered. “This is courtin’… not barn raisin’.”
When Eli arrived, Hannah was outside, hanging laundry with the focus of someone trying very hard not to look toward the road every three seconds.
“Good evening, Hannah,” Eli said.
“Good evening… Eli.”
A silence followed.
A long one.
A very Amish one.
Somewhere in the distance, a chicken clucked.
Respectfully.
“I noticed,” Eli began carefully, “your family’s gate hinge… it no longer squeaks.”
Hannah nodded. “It has not squeaked… since you fixed it.”
Another pause.
Even longer this time.
Historians would later refer to it as “The Pause.”
Finally, Eli took a deep breath.
“Hannah… would you… that is to say… might you consider… possibly… if it is agreeable… and not too forward…”
He stopped.
Reset.
Tried again.
“Walkin’?”
Hannah’s heart soared.
“Yes,” she said, with great composure. “Walkin’ would be… acceptable.”
They walked along the cornfield as the sun set in what could only be described as an aggressively romantic fashion.
The corn stood tall and noble.
The breeze was suspiciously perfect.
Even the bugs seemed to hum in approval.
At last, Eli stopped.
“Hannah,” he said, placing one hand on a particularly trustworthy-looking fence post, “a man builds many things.”
She nodded solemnly.
“Fences,” he continued.
“Yes.”
“Barns.”
“Of course.”
“Exceptionally sturdy shelving.”
“Very important.”
He looked at her.
“But there is one thing… a man cannot build alone.”
Hannah gasped quietly.
“A double-seat buggy?” she guessed.
Eli blinked. “Well—yes—but also…”
He steadied himself.
“A life. A home. A future with… adequate storage.”
Hannah placed a hand over her heart.
This was happening.
This was truly happening.
“I have prayed,” Eli said, “and considered… and organized my thoughts into a very reasonable internal structure.”
She nodded, impressed.
“And I believe… it would be most efficient—”
He stopped, shook his head.
“No. Not efficient.”
He looked at her with rare boldness.
“Right.”
“Hannah Stoltzfus,” he said, voice firm now, “would you… court me?”
The wind hushed.
The corn leaned in.
Somewhere, a cow felt emotional without knowing why.
Hannah smiled—wide, radiant, almost inappropriate for such a modest setting.
“Yes, Eli Zook,” she said. “I would very much like to court.”
They stood there for a moment, basking in the glow of mutual understanding and extremely responsible romantic decision-making.
Then Eli nodded.
“Good.”
Hannah nodded back.
“Good.”
And just like that, it began.

A love story built not on grand gestures or wild passion…
…but on shared glances…
quiet walks…
and the unshakable promise…
that their future shelves would be exceptionally well-built.
